## Preregistration

The purpose of this experiment is to better understand the relationships among welfare valuation and two social emotions: gratitude and anger. All else equal, gratitude is elicited in response to acts of benefit delivery, whereas anger is elicited in response to acts of cost imposition. Using anger as an example, welfare valuation between two actors (A and B) may play a role in anger for two reasons: 1) To the extent that A values B's welfare, costs imposed on A by B will be attenuated by the indirect benefits that A has obtained by the action by valuing B's welfare, and anger may therefore be attenuated; or 2) To the extent that B's actions reveal to A that B does not value A's welfare as much as A expected, A will become angry because A's expectations were negatively violated. In many respects, gratitude could be viewed as being due to actions that are opposite those that cause anger (i.e., due to increases in net benefits or due to positively violated expectations). Thus, the main goal of this experiment is to test whether the former explanation (here we call it the "net cost hypothesis") or the latter explanation (here we call it the "expectation violation" hypothesis) better predicts anger and gratitude.

We aim to recruit 500 non-suspicious subjects via Amazon's Mechanical Turk. Suspicion will be assessed with subjects' responses during debriefing, and subjects who do not believe they have really interacted with another subject will be excluded from all analyses. We will recruit subjects until either (a) we have 500 total non-suspicious subjects or (b) subject payments have reached our budget of $3500. 

In this first experiment, subjects will briefly engage in unscripted communication with another subject in a chat room. Following the brief interaction, all further actions will be scripted (unbeknownst to subjects, who will be led to believe they are still interacting with the person).

Subjects will then fill out a series of money-allocation preferences which were designed to assess welfare valuation (aka, Welfare Tradeoff Ratio; WTR). The questionnaire will assess the subject's WTR for the other subject, as well as the subject's expectations regarding the other subject's WTR for him/herself.

Following the questionnaire, subjects will be "randomly" assigned to be the recipient in a vague economic game, which has properties similar to that of a Dictator Game. In this game, subjects will see a choice that was made by the other subject, which reveals information in one of two ways: 1) When eliciting gratitude (half of subjects), subjects will see that the other subject paid some amount to provide the subject with a benefit; or 2) When eliciting anger (half of subjects), subjects will see that the other subject imposed some cost on the subject to gain money for him/herself. These revealed decisions produce a "revealed WTR" that the partner holds for the subject.

Next, subjects will provide self-report measures of emotions toward the other person. Randomly mixed among distractors, the items we will use to create a scale of anger are "angry," "mad," and "outraged," and the items we will use to create a scale of gratitude are "grateful," "thankful," and "appreciative."

Following the emotion questions, subjects will complete follow-up measures to the same two WTR scales as before. Finally, subjects will answer debriefing questions that probe for suspicion.

This experiment will provide us with data that will disambiguate whether gratitude is primarily elicited by positively violated expectations or by overall net benefits (i.e., direct benefits from the act, discounted by the indirect costs paid by virtue of some degree of welfare interdependence with the other subject). Further, this experiment will provide us with data that will disambiguate whether anger is primarily elicited by negatively violated expectations or by the overall net costs (i.e., direct costs from the act, discounted by the indirect benefits gained by virtue of some degree of welfare interdependence with the other subject).

If we find no differences between the two models for each of these social emotions, then it may actually be direct benefits and direct costs that elicit gratitude and anger, respectively. For simplicity (both from data analytic and experimental design perspectives), we are keeping the direct costs/benefits to the subject fixed, which limits our ability to provide positive support for direct costs/benefits accounts for anger and gratitude.

Our main analyses will be two regression models: one predicting anger and one predicting gratitude. Each model will contain two predictors and their interaction: Net cost/benefit to the subject (defined as the cost/benefit the subject received, plus the cost/benefit the partner received times the subject's WTR for the partner) and the difference in expected WTR (i.e., the subject's assessment of the partner's WTR toward the subject minus revealed WTR). We will also conduct supplementary analyses testing whether change in WTRs predicts anger and gratitude.

## Packages and Data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(MplusAutomation)

ggsc_exp1 <- read.csv("ggsc_exp1.csv", header = T) %>% 
  # create simple composite of gratitude for censored regression
  ## As well as other predictor variables
  rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(gratitude = mean(c(Grateful, Thankful, Appreciative)),
         cost = WTR_reveal*.93,
         w_cost = WTRso0_est*WTR_reveal*.93,
         net_ben = .93 - w_cost,
         exp_viol = WTR_reveal - WTRos0_est,
         wtros_change = WTRos1_est - WTRos0_est,
         wtrso_change = WTRso1_est - WTRso0_est) %>% 
  ungroup()

grat.dat.ns <- ggsc_exp1 %>% filter(condition == "benefit" & Exclude_susp == 0)
```

## Demographic Information

```{r}
nrow(ggsc_exp1[ggsc_exp1$condition == "benefit",])
summary(ggsc_exp1[ggsc_exp1$condition == "benefit",]$sex)
summary(ggsc_exp1[ggsc_exp1$condition == "benefit",]$age)
sd(ggsc_exp1[ggsc_exp1$condition == "benefit",]$age)
nrow(grat.dat.ns)
grat.dat.ns %>% group_by(sex) %>% summarise(n = n())
range(grat.dat.ns$age)
mean(grat.dat.ns$age)
sd(grat.dat.ns$age)
```

## Mplus Output

```{r include = F}
mplus_out <- MplusAutomation::readModels(target = "Mplus", quiet = T)

```

### Benefit-centered models

#### Equation 1. Gratitude Predicted by Benefit

We did not vary the benefit received in Experiment 1. For results of this type of model, see Experiment 2.

#### Equation 2. Gratitude Predicted by Cost

```{r}
model2_params <- mplus_out$model_2_cost.out$parameters$unstandardized %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(grepl("ON", paramHeader))

model2_params_std <- mplus_out$model_2_cost.out$parameters$stdyx.standardized %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(grepl("ON", paramHeader)) %>% 
  select(paramHeader, param, beta = est)

model2_params_ci <- mplus_out$model_2_cost.out$parameters$ci.unstandardized %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(grepl("ON", paramHeader)) %>% 
  select(paramHeader, param, low2.5, up2.5)

model2_params_r2 <- mplus_out$model_2_cost.out$parameters$r2 %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(param == "GRATUDE") %>% 
  mutate(param = "COST") %>% 
  select(param, R2 = est)

model2_results <- full_join(model2_params, model2_params_std) %>% 
  full_join(., model2_params_ci) %>% 
  full_join(., model2_params_r2) %>% 
  unite(Model, c(paramHeader, param), sep = ".")

```

#### Adjudicating Models 9 & 10


```{r}
model10b_params <- mplus_out$model_10_wtr_change_2.out$parameters$unstandardized %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(grepl("ON", paramHeader))

  filter(grepl("ON", paramHeader)) %>% 
  select(paramHeader, param, beta = est)

model10b_params_ci <- mplus_out$model_10_wtr_change_2.out$parameters$ci.unstandardized %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(grepl("ON", paramHeader)) %>% 
  select(paramHeader, param, low2.5, up2.5)

model10b_params_r2 <- mplus_out$model_10_wtr_change_2.out$parameters$r2 %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(param == "GRATUDE") %>% 
  select(param, R2 = est)

model10b_results <- full_join(model10b_params, model10b_params_std) %>% 
  full_join(., model10b_params_ci) %>% 
  full_join(., model10b_params_r2) %>% 
  unite(Model, c(paramHeader, param), sep = ".") %>% 
  fill(R2, .direction = "up") %>% 
  filter(Model != "NA.GRATUDE")

model10b_results
```

## Censored Regression

```{r}
library(censReg)
```


### Benefit and Cost-centered models

#### Model 1. Gratitude Predicted by Benefit

We did not vary the benefit received in Experiment 1. For results of this type of model, see Experiment 2.

#### Model 2. Gratitude Predicted by Costs to Actor

```{r}
grat_cost_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ cost, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_cost_cr)
```

#### Model 3. Gratitude Predicted by Indirect Cost to Actor

```{r}
grat_wcost_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ w_cost, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_wcost_cr)
```

#### Model 4. Gratitude Predicted by net-Benefit

```{r}
grat_ben_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ net_ben, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_ben_cr)
```


### *Perceived* Social Valuation of Self by Other

#### Model 5. Gratitude Explained by Revealed WTR

```{r}
grat_reveal_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ WTR_reveal, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_reveal_cr)
```

#### Model 6. Gratitude predicted by updated perceived WTR

```{r}
grat_wtros_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ WTRos1_est, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_wtros_cr)
```


#### Model 7. Gratitude predicted by Expectation Violations

```{r}
grat_expviol_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ exp_viol, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_expviol_cr)
```


#### Model 8. Gratitude predicted by change in perceived WTR

```{r}
grat_dwtros_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ wtros_change, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_dwtros_cr)
```


#### Model 9. Gratitude predicted by updated WTR

```{r}
grat_postwtrso_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ WTRso1_est, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_postwtrso_cr)
```


#### Model 10. Gratitude explained by change in WTR(self->other)

```{r}
grat_dwtrso_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ wtrso_change, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_dwtrso_cr)
```

#### Adjudicating between Models 9 & 10

```{r}
grat_adj_cr <- censReg(gratitude ~ WTRso0_est + WTRso1_est, left = -Inf, right = max(grat.dat.ns$gratitude), data = grat.dat.ns)

summary(grat_adj_cr)

```

model5_params_ci <- mplus_out_susp$model_5_wtr_reveal.out$parameters$ci.unstandardized %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(grepl("ON", paramHeader)) %>% 
  select(paramHeader, param, low2.5, up2.5)

model5_params_r2 <- mplus_out_susp$model_5_wtr_reveal.out$parameters$r2 %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(param == "GRATUDE") %>% 
  mutate(param = "WTR_REVEAL") %>% 
  select(param, R2 = est)

model5_results <- full_join(model5_params, model5_params_std) %>% 
  full_join(., model5_params_ci) %>% 
  full_join(., model5_params_r2) %>% 
  unite(Model, c(paramHeader, param), sep = ".")

model5_results
